"I don’t have a base case...We’ll get inflation. We’ll get another jobs report...Let’s see where the economy goes," Barkin told journalists after a local chamber of commerce event. "I am not going to predict...We are going to get to the meeting and figure it out." ... AI investment is a main prop of US economic growth right now but is also considered by many central bank policymakers as adding to inflation that remains well above the Fed’s 2% target. Investors currently expect the Fed to raise rates at the December 8-9 meeting as a way to put more downward pressure on the pace of price increases. As it stands, Barkin said in remarks to the Greater Greer Chamber of Commerce in South Carolina, businesses continue to face rising costs and say they are planning to try to pass them along. After nearly six years in which inflation has been above the Fed’s 2% target, "the risk lies on the inflation side of our dual mandate," Barkin said. items.title: Treasury yields rise as investors await October CPI and producer prices
items.excerpt: U.S. Treasury yields rose on Monday as investors awaited a consumer price index report for October early Tuesday, following especially strong employment data last Friday. The two together, along with wholesale inflation numbers set for Friday, may help show the future path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The yield on the 2-year Treasury Add To Watchlist note, which more closely follows short-term Fed rate decisions, climbed more than 4 basis points, to 4.564%. 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist note yields — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — added almost 2 basis points, to 4.876%. The 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist bond yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was higher by less than 1 basis point, at 5.264%. ... Traders are looking ahead to the CPI data, scheduled for release at 8:30 am ET Tuesday, for insight into the pace of inflationary pressure in the economy. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect a 0.3% rise in October's consumer price index. Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, is expected to show an advance of 0.2% on the month. The October U.S. product price index report, a measure of inflation at the wholesale level, is due on Friday. Both reports follow stronger-than-expected U.S. employment numbers last week, which sent Treasury yields higher Friday. Monthly non-farm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, far beyond the 59,000 expected by economists. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. "With inflation elevated and the economy on solid footing, we expect the Federal Reserve to remain focused on the inflation side of its dual mandate and to deliver another 0.25-percentage-point interest-rate increase in December," said Brock Weimer, investment strategy analyst at Edward Jones. In one good sign for policymakers, energy prices moved lower on Monday. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for December delivery slipped more than 5% to $86 per barrel, after President Donald Trump said fresh Iran attacks were "highly unlikely" as talks aimed at resolving the Middle East conflict continue.

items.title: Hot U.S. inflation hasn't cooled off. Rising consumer prices to keep Fed rate hike on track. | Morningstar
items.excerpt: Provided by Dow Jones Nov 9, 2026, 6:16:00 PM By Jeffry Bartash Rising prices point to the Fed increasing borrowing costs before Christmas Americans are fed up with persistent inflation and high gas prices. The Federal Reserve seems all but certain to raise interest rates again soon unless inflation has suddenly cooled off - and there's no sign of that happening. The consumer-price index for October, due out Tuesday morning, is expected to confirm inflation remained still stubbornly high. Here's what to watch in the CPI report - including one big catch. Wall Street forecast Consumer prices probably rose 0.3% in October, just half as much as the increase in September. Lower oil prices (CL00) (BRN00) lent a helping hand for a more mild increase. Yet even a 0.3% increase in the CPI is evidence of persistent inflation. It suggest prices are rising at a yearly 3.5%-plus rate - far above the Fed's 2% annual inflation target. The so-called core rate of inflation, meanwhile, likely rose 0.2% last month, economists polled by the Wall Street Journal forecast. That's still somewhat uncomfortable for the Fed. The core rate is viewed as a better predictor of future inflation. It's been running between 2.5% and 2.9% for most of this year. Missing in action What the October CPI won't tell investors - officially, that is - is how much inflation has risen in the past 12 months. How come? A record-long government shutdown last year prevented the Bureau of Labor Statistics from a compiling the CPI report for the first time in history. It's just a blank in the record books. But no matter: The rate of inflation hasn't changed much. The CPI rose at a 3.7% pace in the 12 months ended in September. The core rate was up 2.6% in the same span. The absence of the October 2025 CPI means those estimates are probably slightly undercounting inflation. It won't be until the December CPI that the effects of the 2025 government shutdown are largely in the rearview mirror. Tariffs and AI Economists say the effect of the Trump tariffs on inflation are receding, but the massive boom in spending on artificial intelligence is now putting upward pressure on the prices of goods. The cost of goods - minus food and energy - rose 0.7% in the 12 months ended in September. That might not sound like much, but goods prices fell in most years in the decade before the pandemic. Goods prices were also falling, not rising, before the Trump administration in the spring of 2025 put in place in the biggest tariffs since World War II. Services The cost of services, especially housing, has been the biggest source of inflation until the surge in oil prices this year tied to the Iran war. The cost of services are rising slightly faster compared to prepandemic trends, but they are less worrisome now than they were a few years ago. Service prices rose 3.1% in the 12 months ended in September, not far from the average 2.8% annual increase from 2015 to 2019. Service costs probably aren't going to slow much further, however, or bring any more relief on inflation. Fed reaction The Fed is widely expected to raise interest rates again in December, following up on its last rate hike in September. An improving labor market and rapidly growing economy could help seal the deal. "In the wake of a blowout jobs report and other signs of a resilient economy, the Fed is going to have little patience with inflation," said BeiChen Lin, senior investment strategist at Russell Investment. Investors put the odds of a rate hike next month at more than 80%, CME Group's FedWatch shows. About the only thing that might stop the Fed would be a shockingly small increase - or no increase at all - in the October CPI. Don't count on it.

items.title: BLS will omit 12-month CPI, Core CPI figures from October report By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com -- The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release its consumer price index report for October on Tuesday without the standard 12-month percentage change figures. The missing data stems from the 2025 government shutdown, which prevented BLS from collecting portions of price data for October 2025. The agency was unable to obtain that information retroactively, according to BLS spokesperson Cody Parkinson. The CPI report typically shows price changes compared to both the previous month and the prior year. The 12-month figure, which was 3.7% in September, is generally how the public understands inflation. Without the October 2025 data, BLS cannot calculate the 12-month percentage change for either the overall CPI or the core measure that excludes food and energy prices. Real earnings growth from a year earlier, a separate but related release, will also be unavailable. The report will still include month-over-month comparisons. Economists expect the CPI rose 0.3% in October from the previous month, while core CPI increased 0.2%.

items.title: U.S. consumer prices seen rising 3.8% year-on-year in October - Truflation By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com - U.S. consumer prices are estimated to have risen by 3.8% in the twelve months to October and 0.3% month-on-month, amid ongoing upward pressure from elevated energy costs caused by the Iran war, according to Truflation predictions. ... Stripping out volatile items like food and fuel, the so-called "core" gauge is seen standing at 2.8% year-on-year and 0.2% month-on-month, the alternative data provider said in a statement. "Headline inflation is moderating, but upstream inflation pipeline remains active. Energy and tariffs are supporting renewed goods inflation. The key risk heading into 2027 is whether rising supply costs spread into persistent core inflation before consumer price sensitivity and moderating labor costs can offset them," Truflation said. The group added that it expects "uneven inflation" through the end of the year and early into 2027, with heightened goods prices due to tariffs and input expenses partially offset by stable services costs. Levies are seen pushing retail prices higher, although grocery prices are anticipated to fall because of retailer discounting and improving supplies. Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, Truflation flagged. For October, the group projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline in particular climbing 37.7%. Month-on-month, gas price growth is tipped to moderate to 0.3%.

items.title: Trump administration live updates: Congress returns with government funding atop the to-do list
items.excerpt: November 09, 2026, 3:50 PM EST By NBC News ## What to know today - CONGRESS IS BACK: Congress returns today for a lame-duck session after Democrats delivered a crushing defeat to Republicans in the midterm elections. The first order of business on the tall list of tasks is funding the government to avert a shutdown in December. - HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT EFFORT: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. war with Iran and other military actions ordered by President Donald Trump. - SENATE LEADERSHIP: A growing number of Republican senators are calling for a delay in their leadership elections tomorrow morning to discuss contenders' plans after the GOP's midterm losses. - UNCALLED RACES: Vote counting continues in the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi, where Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom narrowly lead their respective Republican opponents, Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith. ... ## Rep. Thomas Massie unveils impeachment articles against Hegseth Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., today unveiled articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. If Massie introduces the impeachment articles as privileged, he will force a House floor vote by Wednesday. Massie says he will bring eight charges, including three charges related to allegations that Hegseth violated sections of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. The first article "charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat," Massie's press release said. "It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception." Rep. Thomas Massie. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Article 1 of the Constitution says that Congress has the power to declare war. The last time Congress formally declared war, though, was World War II. The War Powers Resolution says that any time the military is used and war hasn't been declared, the president has to formally notify the House Speaker and Senate president pro tempore within two days. The president must also end the use of armed forces within 60 days if the president uses the military without prior notification to Congress, according to the resolution. The articles of impeachment that Massie introduced also include charges related to alleged "extrajudicial killings," referring to the strikes on alleged drug boats; "kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader," referring to the U.S. capturing now-former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro; and "unlawful war in Yemen." "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate." Hegseth plans to hold a press conference tomorrow morning to address the impeachment efforts.

items.excerpt: ### James Bond: Denis Villeneuve stops just short of naming the next 007 - What happened: Accepting his honour at LACMA’s Art+Film Gala in Los Angeles on Saturday 7 November, Villeneuve told the audience: “With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The new James Bond is…” before adding, “and I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” The Hollywood Reporter reported. On the red carpet he told Variety he was having a “great time” with the casting but named no one - Where the search stands: Nobody has been cast. Deadline reports, citing insiders, that Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult took part in final screen tests. Amazon MGM Studios has not confirmed any name. Deadline says most expect a decision by the end of November, potentially before US Thanksgiving on 26 November. Treat all of this as reporting, not a decision ... ### Dante’s Inferno becomes extreme horror as The Divine Comedy wraps ... - What happened: Anxur Films, with Skincrawl Studios, has wrapped principal photography on The Divine Comedy, the new horror film from Chilean director Patricio Valladares (Hidden in the Woods), FANGORIA reported, debuting a first teaser and stills - The story: A brutal reimagining of Dante’s Inferno. Grieving writer Dante is offered a chance to bring back his late wife, Beatrice, and descends into the realm of the dead guided by Virgil, a former priest. As they go deeper, they realise something in the abyss knows exactly why Dante has come - Who’s in it: Christopher Rygh (Vikings: Valhalla) leads, with Matthew Metcalfe, Tilda Metsola and Fadhillah Othman - The tone: The filmmakers cite Clive Barker’s Hellraiser and Xavier Gens’ Frontier(s) as touchstones, promising physical horror pushed to its limits. It is expected next year - UK availability: UK date not yet confirmed ... ### Report: Jeremy Allen White met Marvel, but Wolverine isn’t in the X-Men script ... - What’s being reported: The Bear star Jeremy Allen White is said to have met Marvel Studios about potentially playing Wolverine, according to reporter Jeff Sneider, as reported by ComicBookMovie.com - The clarification: Sneider has since said White is not actually in talks to play Wolverine, and that Logan is not currently in the script for Jake Schreier’s X-Men reboot. Marvel has not commented ... - What’s new: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary took $8.8 million in its fourth weekend, down just 23%, and now stands at $80 million in North America, Variety reported. That puts it above March of the Penguins ($77 million) and behind only Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 ($119 million) among non-music documentaries - For A24: It is the company’s third-biggest domestic release, behind Backrooms and Marty Supreme, on a $7 million production budget - Who made it: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim direct the near three-hour film, which follows Holmes over three years as she prepares for her 11-year prison sentence.

items.excerpt: ### Godzilla Minus Zero’s record opening, Ramayana’s ₹500 crore Diwali weekend, a strong start for Wild Horse Nine & I Play Rocky, and a Bond announcement due. Morning, all. Monday means the weekend box office, and a Japanese monster has broken a North American record. The weekend box office, worldwide: Godzilla Minus Zero topped the worldwide chart with an estimated $63 million, made up of a record-setting $31.6 million from 3,254 cinemas in North America, plus about $17 million in Japan over the weekend, and the rest from other markets. It’s the biggest-ever North American opening for a live-action foreign-language film, beating the $17.8 million of China’s Hero in 2002, and IMAX generated $21.3 million globally, or 34% of the takings. India’s Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, as it’s known abroad, was second worldwide with about $52 million, according to Screen’s figures, although Deadline has it at $55 million. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine opened to $6 million in North America from 1,100 cinemas, in eighth place, and $6.6 million from 29 other markets, a $12.6 million worldwide start. Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat was second in North America with $20.5 million, plus another $10 million internationally, which is a disappointment against a $92 million budget, although audiences gave it an ‘A’ CinemaScore. Elsewhere, Amazon MGM’s I Play Rocky opened in just seven cinemas in North America, taking $345,000 for a strong $49,200 per-cinema average, and You Can See Everything fell just 23% in its fourth weekend to $8.8 million, taking it to $79.8 million in North America. These are Sunday studio estimates, with the confirmed numbers due later today. ... What I can tell you is that Wicker held up well in its second weekend, with an estimated $1.5 million, down 33%, from 719 cinemas, taking it to $5.7 million. Ramayana’s Diwali weekend: Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 passed a worldwide gross of ₹499.20 crore (about $52 million) after four days, according to Sacnilk, and it’s now just short of ₹500 crore. After a 26% drop on Friday, it bounced back 45% on Saturday, with ₹69.80 crore net in India (about $7.3 million), followed by ₹56.15 crore (about $5.8 million) on Diwali Sunday. That took its India net total to ₹238.85 crore (about $25 million), but narrowly missed the all-time top ten opening weekends in India. It opens in Hong Kong on Thursday, and I’ll bring you the full numbers once the figures settle.
